title: Beyond Views: Measuring and Predicting Engagement in Online Videos
extended_summary:
This paper asks how to measure engagement in online videos more accurately than simple view counts, and whether such engagement can be predicted from publicly available information before a video is uploaded. The authors argue that watch time and watch percentage better capture audience behavior than popularity alone, and they study how these measures relate to video length, stability over time, and perceived video quality.

To do this, they analyze a large-scale YouTube dataset of 5.3 million videos collected via Twitter mentions, along with smaller high-quality comparison sets from Vevo, Billboard, and news channels. They introduce an engagement map that calibrates watch percentage against video duration, and define a new metric called relative engagement based on a video's rank within its duration bin. They also build regression models using video context, Freebase topics, and channel history to predict watch percentage and relative engagement in a cold-start setting.

The study finds that view count and watch time often diverge, especially across categories, and that relative engagement is more stable over time than raw popularity. Videos judged to be high quality by external sources tend to have higher relative engagement. Finally, the authors show that engagement is moderately predictable from pre-upload features, with channel history being the strongest predictor and topic/context features adding some signal. The paper concludes that engagement metrics can be useful for ranking, recommendation, and content production decisions, though the results are based only on publicly available videos and aggregate audience data.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed large-scale observational measurement/prediction paper, not an experimental evaluation of an educational intervention. It provides correlational evidence only, with no K-12 implementation or causal identification.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate Khanmigo or any K-12 science learning outcome, so it offers no direct evidence of impact for the requested research topic.
